title: Intellectual Disability: Levels and Care
body:
## What it is
Intellectual disability (older term: mental retardation) is below-average thinking ability together with limits in everyday adaptive skills, starting in childhood. Severity is graded by IQ and, more usefully, by how much support the person needs.

## Must-know facts
- Moderate: IQ about 40-54, called trainable. Can learn vocational skills such as cooking or sewing.
- Severe: IQ about 25-39, needs close supervision. Can be taught basic activities of daily living such as brushing teeth and dressing.
- Profound: IQ below 25, needs custodial care. Totally dependent on others.
- Mild (not in the source slice): usually called educable, able to learn reading and writing. The IQ band is commonly about 55-70; confirm in your textbook.
- Education focus for the educable client: reading, writing and basic arithmetic.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Keep the person safe and meet basic needs first (feeding, hygiene, protection), especially at the severe and profound levels.
2. Match teaching to the level of function, not the age. Break tasks into small steps.
3. Use repetition: skills are learned by doing the same step many times.
4. Use role modelling: show the skill, then let the client copy it.
5. Restructure the environment (simple, consistent, labelled, free of hazards) rather than expecting the client to adapt.
6. Praise every success; support the family.

## How the exam asks about it
Match the IQ band to the label (trainable, close supervision, custodial) and pick the teaching goal that fits the level. Trap: planning academic teaching for a severe or profound client.

## Memory aid
Made up: "educable reads, trainable works, severe dresses, profound is carried."

## Related topics
[[Developmental Disorders]], [[General Psychiatric Disorders]], [[Therapeutic Communication]]

## Check against your textbook
- The mild range and the exact IQ cut-offs differ by manual; newer manuals grade by adaptive function rather than IQ alone.

title: Anxiolytic Drugs and Cognitive-Behavioral Techniques for Anxiety
body:
## What it is
Two treatment arms for anxiety disorders: antianxiety drugs (mainly benzodiazepines) and cognitive-behavioral techniques that change how the client thinks and acts.

## Must-know facts
- Benzodiazepine examples in the handout: diazepam, oxazepam, chlordiazepoxide, clorazepate and alprazolam. Buspirone and SSRIs are used for generalized anxiety; antidepressants and group therapy also help.
- Side effects: drowsiness, sedation, poor coordination, impaired memory and a clouded sensorium. This is why falls and driving matter.
- Alcohol and caffeine interfere; benzodiazepines add to alcohol's depressant effect.
- Cognitive-behavioral techniques:
  - Positive reframing: turn a catastrophic thought ("my heart is pounding, I will die") into a coping thought ("this is anxiety, it will pass").
  - Decatastrophizing: the therapist asks "what is the worst that could happen, is it likely, could you survive it?" to judge the situation realistically.
  - Thought stopping: break the cycle of negative thoughts with a jolt, such as splashing the face with water or snapping a rubber band on the wrist.
  - Assertiveness training: use "I" statements ("I feel angry when you turn your back while I am talking") to state needs and gain control.
  - Systematic desensitization: gradual exposure to the feared object while relaxed, used for phobias.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Safety first: sedation and unsteadiness mean fall precautions and no driving.
2. Teach: avoid alcohol, caffeine and other sedating drugs; do not stop suddenly after long use.
3. Teach the client to name a thought, challenge it and replace it.
4. Priority diagnosis: ineffective individual coping.

## How the exam asks about it
Name the technique from a one-line example, and pick the teaching point about alcohol or sedation.

## Related topics
[[Anxiety and Anxiety Disorders]], [[Phobic and Somatic Symptom Disorders]], [[Therapeutic Communication]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says to give anxiolytics before meals because food delays absorption and calls them "incompatible with any drugs": both are over-simplified; confirm timing and interactions for each drug.

title: Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa: Findings and Treatment
body:
## What it is
A side-by-side look at the two classic eating disorders, with the signs, lab clues and treatment aims the exam likes.

## Must-know facts
- Anorexia nervosa: refusal or inability to keep a minimally normal weight (about 85 percent of expected), intense fear of fatness, distorted body image and denial of seriousness.
- Anorexia findings: amenorrhea, cold intolerance, lethargy, emaciation, low blood pressure, temperature and pulse, constipation, abdominal pain, enlarged salivary glands, raised BUN, leukopenia, mild anemia and raised liver tests. Mood is low and the client withdraws socially.
- Subtypes: restricting, and binge-purge (self-induced vomiting or misuse of laxatives, enemas and diuretics).
- Bulimia nervosa: binge eating (large amount in a short period, about two hours or less) followed by compensation, at least twice a week for three months. Weight is usually normal.
- Bulimia findings: tooth enamel loss and a ragged "moth-eaten" look, dental caries, esophageal tears, laxative dependence, menstrual irregularity, mildly raised amylase, metabolic alkalosis from vomiting and metabolic acidosis from diarrhea or laxatives. Alcohol and stimulant use are common.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Stabilize physical status: fluids, electrolytes, heart rate and rhythm (Maslow: physiologic first).
2. Restore weight and nutrition with a set plan; rehydrate.
3. Use a calm, matter-of-fact manner with positive expectations; behavior modification with clear rules.
4. Support coping with anxiety and build self-esteem.
5. Common diagnoses: body image disturbance, self-esteem disturbance, ineffective individual coping.

## Treatment and medications
- The handout lists amitriptyline and cyproheptadine for weight gain and olanzapine for weight gain with an antipsychotic effect; antidepressants (desipramine, imipramine, nortriptyline, phenelzine) for bulimia; individual therapy.

## How the exam asks about it
Tell anorexia from bulimia by weight and behavior, and choose the physiologic priority over body-image talk.

## Related topics
[[Eating Disorders]], [[Antidepressants and Mood Stabilizers]], [[Major Depressive Disorder]]

## Check against your textbook
- Drug choices are old-fashioned: current texts favor SSRIs such as fluoxetine for bulimia, and no drug is first line for anorexia. The weight cut-off and refeeding steps vary by source.
outlineRefs: Common nursing diagnoses related to eating disorders

title: Paraphilias
body:
## What it is
Paraphilias are patterns of sexual arousal to unusual objects, situations or people. They become a disorder when they cause distress or harm, or involve someone who cannot or does not consent.

## Must-know facts
- Non-coercive (involve only the person or consenting activity):
  - Fetishism: arousal from objects (shoes, leather, rubber) or body parts (feet, hair).
  - Autoerotic asphyxia: neck constriction to heighten arousal; often ends in accidental death.
  - Sexual masochism: arousal from receiving real or imagined pain or humiliation.
  - Transvestic behavior: arousal from wearing clothing of the other sex.
- Coercive (a victim is involved):
  - Exhibitionism: exposing genitals to a stranger.
  - Voyeurism: secretly watching an unaware person in a private act.
  - Frotteurism: rubbing against a non-consenting person.
  - Pedophilia: sexual interest in children.
  - Sadism: arousal from inflicting pain on another.
  - Urophilia and coprophilia: involving urine and feces with a partner.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Protect safety, including that of potential victims; know the legal reporting duties, especially for children.
2. Keep a calm, nonjudgmental, professional manner and set clear limits.
3. Use diversional activities and behavior modification.
4. Refer for specialized therapy.

## How the exam asks about it
Match the term to the description (voyeurism versus exhibitionism versus frotteurism) and pick the nonjudgmental, limit-setting response.

## Memory aid
Made up: "-ism of looking (voyeur), showing (exhibitionist), rubbing (frotteur)."

## Related topics
[[General Psychiatric Disorders]], [[Personality Disorders by Cluster]], [[Behavioral Management, Restraints and De-escalation]]

## Check against your textbook
- Current manuals separate unusual interests from paraphilic disorders; the handout labels (for example "transvestitism") are dated.

title: Mood Disorder Theories and Variants
body:
## What it is
Mood disorders are lasting changes in emotion that show up as depression, mania or both. This note covers the theories of cause and the milder or special forms that sit around major depression and bipolar disorder.

## Must-know facts
- Genetic: one parent with bipolar disorder gives about a 25 percent chance to the child (figure from the handout).
- Aggression turned inward: harsh superego, anger directed at self. Object loss: early loss of a parent (before about age 11). Personality organization: obsessive, oral-dependent or hysterical styles carry more risk.
- Cognitive: negative views of self, future and experience. Learned helplessness: belief that nothing one does matters.
- Biologic: mania linked to high norepinephrine, depression to low.
- Triggers: major life events, loss, fewer coping resources, drastic physical change.
- Mania: elevated, expansive or irritable mood for about a week. Hypomania: at least 4 days, less severe, no psychosis and no major impairment. Mixed episode (handout also calls it rapid cycling; usually these are different, see check section): both poles nearly every day for a week.
- Bipolar I: at least one manic or mixed episode. Bipolar II: major depression plus hypomania, never full mania.
- Dysthymia: milder depression for at least 2 years. Cyclothymia: 2 years of hypomanic and depressive symptoms not meeting full criteria.
- Substance-induced mood disorder: mood change caused directly by a drug or toxin.
- Seasonal affective disorder: fall-winter type brings oversleeping, carbohydrate craving, weight gain; spring-summer type is rarer, with insomnia, poor appetite and weight loss.
- Postpartum: blues (peak days 3-7, fade without treatment), postpartum depression (full depressive episode within weeks), postpartum psychosis (within about 3 weeks, confusion then delusions and hallucinations; an emergency).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Safety for suicide, harm to others and the newborn.
2. Differentiate the episode from the description, then match the response.
3. Treat sleep, nutrition and hydration.

## How the exam asks about it
Pick Bipolar I versus II, hypomania versus mania, and blues versus psychosis from timing and severity.

## Related topics
[[Major Depressive Disorder]], [[Bipolar Disorder and Mania]], [[Antidepressants and Mood Stabilizers]]

## Check against your textbook
- Rapid cycling usually means 4 or more episodes in a year, not a mixed episode. Time criteria differ by manual.
outlineRefs: Common etiological theories of mood disorders

title: Lithium Therapy: Nursing Responsibilities
body:
## What it is
Lithium carbonate is the classic mood stabilizer. It lowers the frequency and depth of manic cycling. Its exact action is unknown; it crosses the blood-brain barrier and the placenta, so it is avoided in pregnancy.

## Must-know facts
- Give with or after meals to reduce stomach upset.
- Benefit takes 10 to 14 days to appear, so acute mania is often covered by another drug at first.
- The handout lists a normal level of 0.5 to 1.5 mEq/L; toxicity signs include severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle weakness and tremor.
- Too little water or sodium (sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, low-salt diet) raises the lithium level and can cause toxicity. Too much water dilutes it.
- Fluids: about 2 to 3 liters daily. Keep salt intake normal and steady.
- Track daily weight, intake and output, and look for dependent edema.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Hold the dose and report if toxicity signs appear; this is urgent.
2. Check blood levels as ordered.
3. Teach steady fluid and salt intake, and to call the provider during vomiting, diarrhea or fever.
4. Manic clients: protect from injury, limit stimulation, give high-calorie finger foods, set limits kindly, and assess for suicidal or violent thoughts.
5. Promote rest with a bedtime routine and a quiet environment.

## How the exam asks about it
Which statement shows the client understands lithium (steady salt and fluids, no stopping suddenly) and which sign needs a call.

## Related topics
[[Antidepressants and Mood Stabilizers]], [[Bipolar Disorder and Mania]], [[Mood Disorder Theories and Variants]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout writes "salt intake 2-3 L/day", which is a clear typo (liters apply to fluids). Mannitol for toxicity is not standard in most sources; check. Many texts give a therapeutic range of about 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L, with toxicity above about 1.5.

title: Somatoform Disorders: Gains, Theories and Management
body:
## What it is
Physical symptoms with no organic cause that fully explains them, arising from psychological conflict and not under the client's conscious control. The distress is real.

## Must-know facts
- Three central features: symptoms suggest a medical illness without a demonstrable cause; psychological factors start, worsen or maintain them; they are not consciously produced.
- Somatization disorder: many symptoms beginning before age 30, lasting years: pain, gastrointestinal, sexual and pseudo-neurologic symptoms.
- Conversion disorder: sudden loss of sensory or motor function (blindness, paralysis); la belle indifference (strangely unconcerned) may appear.
- Pain disorder: pain, often not relieved by analgesics, strongly shaped by emotion.
- Hypochondriasis: fear of having (or catching) a serious disease, from misreading body sensations. Body dysmorphic disorder: preoccupation with an imagined or exaggerated defect.
- Mechanisms: internalization (keeping stress inside) and somatization (expressing it physically), both unconscious.
- Primary gain: relief of anxiety or conflict by having symptoms. Secondary gain: benefits from others, such as attention.
- Biologic view: amplified awareness of normal sensations.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Show empathy, accept complaints and build trust; this keeps the client with one provider rather than "doctor shopping."
2. Do not confront the origin of symptoms until the client has other coping tools.
3. Limit time spent discussing symptoms and avoid reinforcing gains.
4. Teach routine, nutrition, sleep, journaling and expression of feelings.
5. Coping: emotion-focused (relaxation, deep breathing, guided imagery, distraction) and problem-focused (problem solving, role play).
6. Pain: relaxation, imagery, physical therapy, non-steroidal pain relievers; avoid narcotics because of dependence risk.

## Medications
- SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine) mainly for accompanying depression.

## How the exam asks about it
Choose primary versus secondary gain, and the non-confrontational, trust-building response.

## Related topics
[[Phobic and Somatic Symptom Disorders]], [[Freud's Theory and Defense Mechanisms]], [[Malingering, Factitious Disorder and Munchausen Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
- Newer terms: somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety disorder replace several of these labels. Always rule out physical illness first.

title: Malingering, Factitious Disorder and Munchausen Syndrome
body:
## What it is
Conditions where symptoms are deliberately produced or exaggerated. Unlike somatic disorders, the client is aware of the faking, but the reason differs.

## Must-know facts
- Malingering: intentional false or exaggerated symptoms for an outside reward such as avoiding work, escaping prosecution, getting money or obtaining drugs. Symptoms stop when the goal is reached. Not a mental illness.
- Factitious disorder: symptoms feigned or produced just to receive attention and the sick role.
- Munchausen syndrome: a severe form where the person may injure himself or herself to gain care.
- Munchausen by proxy: harming another person (often a child) to gain attention from medical staff or to be a "hero" for saving the victim. This is abuse.
- Somatic disorders differ: symptoms are not consciously produced.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Always assess and treat real physical problems first.
2. For suspected proxy abuse, protect the victim and report according to law and policy.
3. Stay objective and nonjudgmental; document facts, not opinions.
4. Refer to psychiatric care.

## How the exam asks about it
Tell malingering (clear external gain) from factitious (attention) from somatic (unconscious).

## Related topics
[[Somatoform Disorders: Gains, Theories and Management]], [[Phobic and Somatic Symptom Disorders]], [[General Psychiatric Disorders]]

## Check against your textbook
- Reporting duties for suspected abuse follow Philippine law and facility policy; verify locally.

title: Inhalant Use
body:
## What it is
Inhalants are chemicals breathed in for a brief high: gasoline, glue, paint thinner, spray paint, cleaners, correction fluid, spray propellants, solvents (esters, ketones, glycols), anesthetics and nitrates. They can badly damage the brain, nerves and liver.

## Must-know facts
- Intoxication: dizziness, nystagmus, poor coordination, slurred speech, unsteady gait, tremor, weakness, blurred vision, aggression, apathy, poor judgment; stupor and coma may follow.
- Acute toxicity: low oxygen, respiratory depression, vagal stimulation and rhythm problems; death can come from bronchospasm, cardiac arrest, suffocation or aspiration of vomit.
- No antidote. Treatment is support of breathing and the heart until the substance clears.
- No true withdrawal syndrome or detoxification. Long-term effects include persistent dementia and psychosis, anxiety or mood disorders.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway, breathing and circulation first; monitor cardiac rhythm.
2. Prevent aspiration; keep the client safe and calm.
3. Later: counseling, family education, referral.

## How the exam asks about it
Know that there is no antidote or withdrawal treatment, and that support of breathing is the priority.

## Related topics
[[Substance Use Disorders: Basic Concepts]], [[Uppers and Hallucinogens]], [[Downers: Barbiturates and Opioids]]

## Check against your textbook
- Some texts describe mild withdrawal symptoms with heavy chronic use; confirm.

title: Recovery Programs and Drugs Used in Substance Use
body:
## What it is
Long-term help for alcohol and drug problems: peer groups, medications that deter use or ease withdrawal, and nursing education.

## Must-know facts
- Alcoholics Anonymous: peer self-help from the 1930s; the 12-step model holds that total abstinence is essential and that support from others keeps sobriety. Closed meetings are for people seeking recovery; open meetings welcome anyone. Related: Narcotics Anonymous, Al-Anon (spouses, partners, friends) and Alateen (children of parents with substance problems).
- Alcohol: thiamine (vitamin B1) to prevent or treat Wernicke and Korsakoff syndromes; vitamin B12 and folic acid for deficiency; disulfiram deters drinking: alcohol then causes flushing, throbbing headache, sweating, nausea, vomiting, severe hypotension, confusion, coma and possible death.
- Opioids: methadone, a long-acting opioid substitute that meets physical need without cravings for more; levomethadyl (analgesic only for opioid dependence); naltrexone blocks opioid effects; clonidine eases autonomic withdrawal signs (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea); ondansetron treats nausea.
- Opioid overdose is treated with naloxone (see [[Downers: Barbiturates and Opioids]]).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Teach client and family; dispel myths.
2. Reduce codependent behaviors in family and refer them for help.
3. Build coping skills and role-play hard situations.
4. Focus on the here and now; set realistic goals such as "stay sober today."
5. Teach disulfiram users to avoid all hidden alcohol.

## How the exam asks about it
Match drug to purpose (disulfiram, naltrexone, methadone, clonidine) and pick the group (Al-Anon for relatives).

## Related topics
[[Alcohol Use Disorder]], [[Substance Use Disorders: Basic Concepts]], [[Therapeutic Communication]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout calls naltrexone a drug for overdose, which is naloxone's job; naltrexone blocks effects and reduces craving. Levomethadyl is no longer widely available. Check local drug availability.

title: Dissociative Disorders and Grounding Care
body:
## What it is
Dissociation is an unconscious defense that protects a person from the full pain of a horrific event by splitting off memory, identity or awareness. Dissociative disorders disrupt the normal link between consciousness, memory, identity and perception of surroundings.

## Must-know facts
- Dissociative amnesia: cannot recall important personal information, usually stressful or traumatic.
- Dissociative fugue: sudden leaving of home or work, travel, inability to recall past or identity, perhaps a new identity.
- Dissociative identity disorder (formerly multiple personality): two or more distinct identities that take control, with memory gaps.
- Depersonalization disorder: persistent detachment from one's mind or body, but reality testing stays intact; the client is not psychotic.

## Assessment findings
- Hyperalert, startles at small noises, uncomfortable when someone stands close, pacing or curled up with arms around the knees.
- Frightened, may cry, scream or hide. Self-destructive thoughts, possible suicidal ideation.
- Memory gaps, low self-esteem (feels bad or deserving of abuse), trouble trusting.
- Nightmares, sleep trouble, overeating or poor appetite, alcohol or drug use to blot out memories.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Assess suicide and self-harm risk first.
2. Teach the client to go to a safe place during destructive urges and wait for them to pass.
3. Use grounding: remind the client they are in the present, an adult and safe; have them stand and walk, focus on sensory information, breathe deeply and relax.
4. Encourage written feelings at set times and positive distraction (exercise, music, talking, hobbies).
5. See the client as a survivor, not a victim.

## Treatment
- SSRIs such as paroxetine or sertraline; group, individual and cognitive-behavioral therapy aimed at re-association.

## How the exam asks about it
Match the type to the description and choose grounding and safety actions.

## Related topics
[[Trauma and Stressor-Related Disorders]], [[General Psychiatric Disorders]], [[Disturbances in Affect and Memory]]

## Check against your textbook
- The assessment list in the source blends trauma and dissociation signs; fugue is now a specifier of amnesia in current manuals.
